title: When Are Both Roots Integers? x² + bx + 12b | AMC 10-Style Level 4

scenes.visual: L0: x² + bx + 12b with b = −1 dropping in → x² − x − 12 = (x − 4)(x + 3), roots 4 and −3 on a number line. L1: green ticks on both roots, a big '?' over b. L2: Vantee title card.
lines: Put b equals negative one: x squared minus x minus twelve. Its roots are four and negative three.
Both roots are integers! So how many values of b work like that?
Hello, I'm Vantee, and today one clever trick will find them all.

scenes.visual: Prompt card: 'For how many integers b are both roots of x² + bx + 12b = 0 integers?' L2: choices A 8, B 15, C 16, D 30, E 32.
lines: For how many integers b are both roots of x squared plus b x plus twelve b equals zero integers?
Here are the five choices: eight, fifteen, sixteen, thirty and thirty-two.

scenes.visual: L0: number line …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … 'integers'; pills 'b integer', 'both roots integers'. L1: goal pill 'count values of b' (not pairs of roots).
lines: An integer is a whole number: positive, negative or zero. b and both roots must be integers.
We're counting values of b, not pairs of roots.

scenes.visual: Pause card with countdown ring; question and choices visible.
lines: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

scenes.visual: Equation rows on the right. L0: x² + bx + 12b = (x − r)(x − s). L1: = x² − (r + s)x + rs. L2: the two forms stacked, matching terms colour-linked. L3: b = −(r + s) = −r − s. L4: 12b = rs. L5: rs = 12b = −12r − 12s. L6: rs + 12r + 12s = 0.
lines: Welcome back! Call the roots r and s. Then the left side is x minus r, times x minus s.
Multiplying out gives x squared, minus the sum of the roots times x, plus their product.
Match it up! First, b is the negative of the sum: b equals negative r minus s.
Second, twelve b is the product: twelve b equals r times s.
Now let's get rid of b. We know r s equals twelve b, which is negative twelve r minus twelve s.
Move it all to one side: r s plus twelve r plus twelve s equals zero.

scenes.visual: Aha beat. L0: area grid (r + 12) by (s + 12), split into four cells. L1: cells labelled rs, 12r, 12s, 144 (12 × 12 = 144). L2: rs + 12r + 12s + 144 = 144; the 144 cell lights up. L3: (r + 12)(s + 12) = 144, big.
lines: Here's the clever step. Think of r plus twelve, times s plus twelve, as a grid with four parts.
The parts are r s, twelve r, twelve s, and twelve times twelve: one hundred forty-four.
Our equation already has the first three parts. So add one hundred forty-four to both sides.
Now it factors! r plus twelve, times s plus twelve, equals one hundred forty-four.

scenes.visual: Factor-pair table builds row by row (L0–L2): 1×144, 2×72, 3×48, 4×36, 6×24, 8×18, 9×16, 12×12, '8 pairs'. L3: swap arrow 9×16 ↔ 16×9 'same b'. L4: negative column (−1)(−144) … (−12)(−12), '8 more'. L5: r = u − 12, s = v − 12, b = −(r + s) = 24 − (u + v). L6: 9 + 16 = 25 → b = −1, roots −3 and 4. L7: 12 + 12 = 24 → b = 0, x² = 0. L8: b column fills in, all different. L9: 8 + 8 = 16, answer reveal, choice C.
lines: Let's list the factor pairs. One times one hundred forty-four, two times seventy-two.
Three times forty-eight, four times thirty-six, six times twenty-four.
Eight times eighteen, nine times sixteen, and twelve times twelve. That's eight pairs.
Swapping a pair just swaps r and s. Same equation, so the same value of b.
But wait! Two negatives also multiply to a positive. So there are eight negative pairs too.
Each root is its factor minus twelve. So b is twenty-four minus the sum of the pair.
Nine and sixteen add to twenty-five, so b is negative one. That's our opening example!
Twelve and twelve make both roots zero, so b is zero. That counts too!
Different pairs have different sums, so each pair gives its own value of b.
Eight positive pairs plus eight negative pairs is sixteen. That's Choice C!

scenes.visual: Rows. L0: r² + br + 12b = 0. L1: b(r + 12) = −r². L2: d = r + 12, r = d − 12. L3: r² = d² − 24d + 144. L4: bd = −d² + 24d − 144 → b = 24 − d − 144/d. L5: d | 144; divisor list ±1 … ±144, '15 + 15 = 30'. L6: s = −b − r. L7: d = 16 → r = 4, d = 9 → r = −3, both b = −1. L8: d ↔ 144/d pairing arrows; 12 and −12 loop to themselves. L9: 28 ÷ 2 = 14, 14 + 2 = 16. L10: tip card.
lines: Here's another way: chase one root. Plug r in: r squared plus b r plus twelve b equals zero.
Group the b terms: b times r plus twelve equals negative r squared.
Let d be r plus twelve, so r is d minus twelve.
Then r squared is d squared, minus twenty-four d, plus one hundred forty-four.
Divide by d, and b equals twenty-four, minus d, minus one hundred forty-four over d.
So d must divide one hundred forty-four. That gives thirty choices, positive and negative.
The other root, s, is negative b minus r. So it's an integer too.
d is sixteen for the root four, and nine for the root negative three. Both give b negative one.
So the d values pair up. Only twelve and negative twelve pair with themselves.
The other twenty-eight make fourteen pairs. Fourteen plus two is sixteen!
When would you pick this way? If you forget sum and product. One root is enough.

scenes.visual: Choice chips; wrong ones turn red one by one. L0: A 8 → only the positive column; negative column greyed '8 missing'. L1: B 15 → the 15 positive divisors as separate b's; 9 and 16 both → b = −1 circled. L2: D 30 → all 30 divisors, pairs bracketed '×2'. L3: E 32 → 2 × 16 with r ↔ s swap arrow crossed out. L4: habit card 'count values of b, not orders of roots'.
lines: Choice A, eight, counts only the positive pairs. It forgets the eight negative ones.
Choice B, fifteen, treats each positive divisor as its own b. But nine and sixteen share one b.
Choice D, thirty, counts all thirty divisors. Most values of b get counted twice, once per root.
Choice E, thirty-two, is what you'd get by doubling sixteen, as if swapping roots made a new b.

scenes.visual: New question card: 'For how many integers b are both roots of x² + bx + 6b = 0 integers?' No choices.
lines: Ready for a challenge? Now the equation is x squared plus b x plus six b equals zero.
For how many integers b are both roots integers?

scenes.visual: Pause card, countdown, variant question visible.
lines: Pause the video, and go for it!

scenes.visual: Rows. L0: r + s = −b, rs = 6b → rs + 6r + 6s = 0. L1: + 36 → (r + 6)(s + 6) = 36. L2–L3: pairs 1×36, 2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6 and the negative column. L4: 5 + 5 = 10, success reveal + chime at line end. L5: 4×9 → roots −2, 3; b = −1; x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2).
lines: Same steps! The sum is negative b, the product is six b.
Get rid of b, and we get r times s, plus six times r, plus six times s, equals zero.
Add thirty-six to both sides: r plus six, times s plus six, equals thirty-six.
Pairs that make thirty-six: one and thirty-six, two and eighteen, three and twelve.
Four and nine, and six and six. That's five pairs, plus five negative pairs.
Five plus five gives ten values of b!
Check: four and nine give roots negative two and three. Sum one, so b is negative one.
If you got ten, amazing work!

scenes.visual: Summary card: roots → sum & product → remove b → add a constant so it factors → count factor pairs (± both!).
lines: Turn the roots into a sum and a product, then get rid of b.
Add a number so it factors, and count the factor pairs. Don't forget the negative ones!
I'm Vantee. Keep exploring, and I'll see you next time!
